The Wintrodes were Wenderoths of the Palatinate, the Rhineland country around Heidelberg.
For a hundred years it had been a battlefield: the Thirty Years’ War emptied it,
Louis XIV’s armies burned it in 1688 to 89, and the wars went on into the 1700s.
Taxes were heavy, the ruling princes changed the official church more than once,
and the great frost of 1709 killed the vines and orchards.
Pennsylvania offered what the Palatinate did not: good land, cheap, and William Penn’s freedom of worship.
From the 1720s shiploads of Palatines left every year, down the Rhine to Rotterdam,
by way of an English port, and across to Philadelphia — a journey of months that many did not survive,
and that many paid for afterwards with years of bound labour.
Johann Caspar Wenderoth of Bammental and his bride Anna Margaretha landed from the Pleasant in September 1732.
Like many Palatines they moved on to find land, west into Maryland near Frederick,
and their descendants farmed the Adams County border country of Pennsylvania for a century.
